summary: A Segment Routing Policy is an ordered list of segments, with one or more candidate paths. This document extends PCEP so that controllers and routers can create, report and manage SR Policy candidate paths. It updates RFC 8231.

plainLanguage.summary: An SR Policy is a named set of possible routes that a router can send traffic along, and each of those routes is called a candidate path. This document lets a central controller and a router agree on such a policy over PCEP, the protocol they use to talk about paths. It gives the policy an identifier and groups the candidate paths under it, so that a path built by the controller is recognised as belonging to the same policy as one built locally or by BGP.

questions: what is an sr policy association
subtitle: How PCEP describes Segment Routing Policies, so controllers and routers can agree on each candidate path.

tldr.problem: A Segment Routing Policy is a set of candidate paths that a headend router can steer traffic into, and the same policy can be built by a controller, by local configuration or by BGP. The PCEP extensions of RFC 8664 create individual paths but cannot say which of them belong to the same policy.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 9862 maps an SR Policy onto a new PCEP association type, the SR Policy Association, and maps each candidate path onto an LSP inside that association. It defines the association parameters, four TLVs carried in the association, a capability TLV, and three more TLVs carried in the LSP object.
tldr.outcome: The document updates RFC 8231 so that the Path Computation Request and Reply messages become optional for SR Policy paths, and it registers a new association type and eight new PCEP TLVs at IANA. It recommends running these extensions only over authenticated and encrypted PCEP sessions.

today: RFC 9862 is a Proposed Standard published in October 2025, and it has not been obsoleted. It updates RFC 8231, and IANA has registered Association Type 6 for the SR Policy Association, eight new PCEP TLV types and two new registries for the invalidation flags, plus one for the capability flag field.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
The Segment Routing Policy Architecture of RFC 9256 details the concepts of Segment Routing Policy and the approaches for steering traffic into one. The PCEP extensions for Segment Routing in RFC 8664 allow a stateful Path Computation Element to compute and initiate traffic engineering paths, and allow a Path Computation Client to request a path subject to constraints and optimization criteria in an SR domain. Those extensions can create SR traffic engineering paths, but they do not constitute SR Policies as defined in RFC 9256, and they lack support for two things: associating an SR Policy Candidate Path signalled via PCEP with candidate paths of the same SR Policy signalled by other means, such as local configuration or BGP, and associating an SR Policy with an intent via colour, which enables headend-based steering of BGP service routes over SR Policies provisioned via PCEP.

RFC 8697 introduces a generic mechanism for creating a grouping of LSPs, called an Association. This document uses it. An SR Policy is associated with one or more Candidate Paths, and the Candidate Path is the unit for signalling an SR Policy to a headend. The document extends RFC 8664 to support signalling SR Policy Candidate Paths as LSPs, and to signal Candidate Path membership in an SR Policy by means of the Association mechanism. A PCEP Association corresponds to an SR Policy and an LSP corresponds to a Candidate Path. Because the unit of signalling in PCEP is the LSP, all the information related to an SR Policy is carried at the Candidate Path level.

The document also updates Section 5.8.2 of RFC 8231, making the use of the Path Computation Request and Path Computation Reply messages optional for LSPs set up with Path Setup Type 1 for Segment Routing and Path Setup Type 3 for SRv6, with the aim of reducing the number of PCEP message exchanges and simplifying implementation.
sections.plainLanguage: An SR Policy is a named set of possible routes, and each route in the set is a candidate path. The same policy can be built by a central controller, by a router's own configuration, or by BGP, and the router has to recognise that they are the same policy. The PCEP extensions that existed could create paths but had no way to group them, so this document adds a grouping object and gives the policy an identifier that all its candidate paths share.

sections.title: Terminology
sections.content:
The document uses the terms Explicit Route Object, Path Computation Client, Path Computation Element, PCEP Peer and PCEP speaker from RFC 5440, Label Switched Path from RFC 3031, and Border Gateway Protocol Link State from RFC 9552.

It defines the following terms of its own. The Endpoint is the IPv4 or IPv6 endpoint address of an SR Policy. The Color is the 32-bit colour of an SR Policy. The Protocol-Origin is the protocol used to create a Candidate Path, the Originator is the device that created it, and the Discriminator distinguishes Candidate Paths created by the same device. Association parameters are the key data that uniquely identifies an Association, and Association information is the information related to the Association Type. An SR Policy LSP is an LSP set up using Path Setup Type 1 for Segment Routing or 3 for SRv6. The SR Policy Association is a new Association Type used to group the Candidate Paths belonging to the same SR Policy; depending on the context it can refer to the PCEP ASSOCIATION object of an SR Policy type or to the group of LSPs that belong to the association.
sections.plainLanguage: Several names are needed to follow the document. An SR Policy has a colour, a number that expresses its intent, and an endpoint, the address it delivers to. A Candidate Path is described by who made it, with what protocol, and with a number that separates it from other paths from the same maker. The new association object is what groups the candidate paths of one policy.

sections.title: Overview
sections.content:
An SR Policy is represented by a new type of PCEP Association, the SR Policy Association. The SR Policy Candidate Paths of a specific SR Policy are the LSPs within the same association. The extensions specify the encoding of a single segment list within an SR Policy Candidate Path; the encoding of multiple segment lists is outside the scope of the document.

An association carries three pieces of information: the SR Policy Identifier, the SR Policy Candidate Path Identifier, and the SR Policy Candidate Path attributes.

The document also specifies some information that is not encoded as part of an association: the computation priority of the LSP, the Explicit NULL Label Policy for unlabelled IP packets, and the Drop-Upon-Invalid behaviour for traffic steering when the LSP is operationally down.
sections.plainLanguage: An SR Policy is one association object, and the candidate paths inside it are ordinary PCEP paths. Each path carries the policy's identifier, its own identifier, and optional attributes such as a preference value. Three more settings do not belong to the association and are carried on the path itself.

sections.title: Association Parameters
sections.content:
Per RFC 8697, LSPs are associated with other LSPs by adding them to a common association group. That group is uniquely identified by the combination of the Association Type, Association ID, Association Source and, if present, Global Association Source or Extended Association ID. These fields are the association parameters. This document defines a new Association Type, 6, named SR Policy Association.

Capability exchange for the SRPA type must happen before the association is used. A PCEP speaker must include the SRPA type 6 in the ASSOC-Type-List TLV and must receive the same from its peer. An SRPA must be assigned for all SR Policy LSPs by the speaker originating the LSP if the capability was advertised by both speakers. If that condition is not satisfied, the receiving speaker must send a PCErr message with Error-Type 6 Mandatory Object Missing and Error-value 22 Missing SR Policy Association. A given LSP must belong to at most one SRPA, because a Candidate Path cannot belong to multiple SR Policies; a request to join more than one gives Error-Type 26 Association Error and Error-value 7 Cannot join the association group.

An SR Policy is identified through the headend, colour and endpoint tuple. The association parameters are set as follows. The Association Type is 6. The Association Source is set to the headend value of the SR Policy. The Association ID is always the numeric value 1. The Extended Association ID TLV is mandatory for an SRPA and encodes the colour and the endpoint. That TLV has type 31, a length of 8 octets when an IPv4 address is encoded in the Endpoint field and 20 octets when an IPv6 address is, a colour that is an unsigned non-zero 32-bit integer value, and an endpoint that is either an IPv4 or an IPv6 address. The endpoint value may differ from the one in the destination address field of the END-POINTS object, or in the Tunnel Endpoint Address field of the LSP-IDENTIFIERS TLV.

The encoding is chosen so that there is no possibility of a race condition when several PCEP speakers want to associate the same SR Policy at the same time. Because every speaker derives the same association parameters independently from the SR Policy parameters, they all arrive at the same association without negotiating it.

The last hop of a computed Candidate Path may differ from the endpoint in the tuple. One use case is to terminate the SR Policy before reaching the endpoint and have the decapsulated traffic forwarded the rest of the way by the Interior Gateway Protocol shortest paths; the endpoint value is still used at the headend to steer traffic with that address into the policy. The destination of the Candidate Path is signalled using the END-POINTS object or the LSP-IDENTIFIERS TLV as usual, and when neither is present the speaker must take the destination from the Endpoint field of the Extended Association ID TLV. An SR Policy with colour-only steering is signalled with the endpoint set to the unspecified value, 0.0.0.0 for IPv4 or :: for IPv6.
sections.plainLanguage: The association object names the policy in a way every speaker can work out on its own: the router the policy starts at, the colour and the endpoint. Because the values are derived from the policy itself rather than negotiated, two speakers that want to describe the same policy arrive at the same association, with no chance of a race. The identifier of the policy is the same in every candidate path, and a path may belong to only one policy.

sections.title: Association Information TLVs
sections.content:
The association object may carry four TLVs. SRPOLICY-POL-NAME is optional and encodes the SR Policy name string. SRPOLICY-CPATH-ID is mandatory and encodes the SR Policy Candidate Path Identifier. SRPOLICY-CPATH-NAME is optional and encodes the Candidate Path name. SRPOLICY-CPATH-PREFERENCE is optional and encodes the Candidate Path preference value; if the TLV is absent, the default preference is 100.

When a mandatory TLV is missing from an association object, the speaker must send a PCErr message with Error-Type 6 Mandatory Object Missing and Error-value 21 Missing SR Policy Mandatory TLV. Only one instance of each TLV type can be carried in an association object, and only the first occurrence is processed; any others must be silently ignored.

The SRPOLICY-CPATH-ID TLV has type 57 and a length of 28. Its fields are the Protocol-Origin, an 8-bit unsigned value from the SR Policy Protocol Origin registry, a reserved field that must be zero on transmission and ignored on receipt, the Originator Autonomous System Number as a 32-bit unsigned value, the Originator Address as a 128-bit value, and the Discriminator as a 32-bit unsigned value. The discriminator is the field that mainly distinguishes different Candidate Paths coming from the same originator, and it may be any number in the 32-bit range.

The two name TLVs have types 56 and 58. Their values must be strings of printable ASCII characters without a NULL terminator, their length must be greater than zero, and they must be zero-padded so that the TLV is 4-octet aligned, with the padding not included in the length field. The size of the name should be limited to 255 bytes, and implementations may truncate long names to simplify interoperability with other protocols. The preference TLV has type 59 and a length of 4, carrying a 32-bit unsigned value.
sections.plainLanguage: The association can carry the name of the policy, the name of the path, a preference value that says how much the path is preferred, and one mandatory item that identifies the path. That identifier is three numbers: which protocol created the path, which device created it, and a discriminator that separates it from other paths from the same device.

sections.title: Capability Negotiation and Stateless Operation
sections.content:
The mechanisms in Section 5 do not use the association for signalling, so they cannot rely on the Association capability negotiation and need separate capability negotiation. The document specifies four new TLVs carried in the OPEN or LSP object. Only one instance of each type can be carried, only the first occurrence is processed, and any others must be ignored.

The SRPOLICY-CAPABILITY TLV is a TLV for the OPEN object, used at session establishment to learn the peer's capabilities with respect to SR Policy. Implementations that support SR Policy must include it in the OPEN object if the extension is enabled, and the ASSOC-Type-List TLV containing the SRPA type 6 must be present as well. If a speaker receives an SRPA but the SRPOLICY-CAPABILITY TLV was not exchanged, it must send a PCErr message with Error-Type 10 Reception of an invalid object and Error-value 44 Missing SRPOLICY-CAPABILITY TLV, and must then close the PCEP session. The TLV has type 71 and a length of 4. Its flags field is 32 bits, with four flags defined: the P-flag for Computation Priority, the E-flag for Explicit NULL Label Policy, the I-flag for Invalidation and the L-flag for Stateless Operation. When a flag is clear, the receiving speaker must not send the corresponding TLV and must ignore it on receipt. Unassigned bits must be set to zero on transmission and ignored on receipt.

Section 5.3 updates RFC 8231. Section 5.8.2 of that document allows delegation of an LSP in an operationally down state, but mandates the use of PCReq before sending PCRpt. This document makes that section inapplicable to SR Policy LSPs, so a PCC that wants to delegate an SR Policy LSP may proceed directly to sending PCRpt, without first sending PCReq and waiting for PCRep. That reduces the number of PCEP messages and simplifies the implementation. A speaker is not required to support PCReq and PCRep at all for SR Policies: it indicates support through the L-flag. When that flag is cleared, or when the SRPOLICY-CAPABILITY TLV is absent, the peer must not be sent PCReq or PCRep messages for SR Policy LSPs. This applies only to SR Policy LSPs; for other LSP types, such as RSVP-TE LSPs, Section 5.8.2 of RFC 8231 continues to apply.
sections.plainLanguage: The four optional settings are negotiated in the opening message of the session, one flag each, so that neither side sends a setting the other does not understand. The same negotiation decides whether the two sides need the request and reply messages at all for these paths. When they do not, a router can report a path as down with a single report instead of asking first and waiting for a reply.

sections.title: LSP Object TLVs
sections.content:
Three new TLVs are carried in the LSP object. The COMPUTATION-PRIORITY TLV is optional and signals the numerical computation priority, that is, the priority with which this LSP is to be recomputed by the PCE upon a topology change. The lowest value is the highest priority. If the TLV is absent and the P-flag is set, a default priority of 128 is used. The TLV has type 68 and a length of 4.

The EXPLICIT-NULL-LABEL-POLICY TLV is optional and indicates whether an Explicit NULL label must be pushed on an unlabelled IP packet before any other labels, which is necessary to steer such a packet into an SR Policy in the MPLS data plane. If the TLV is not present, the decision is left to local configuration. Explicit NULL is currently only defined for SR-MPLS and not for SRv6, so the receiving speaker must ignore the presence of this TLV for SRv6 policies. The TLV has type 69 and a length of 4, and its value comes from the SR Policy ENLP Values registry.

The INVALIDATION TLV is optional and controls traffic steering into an LSP when the LSP is operationally down. Normally such an LSP stops attracting traffic, and traffic that would have been destined for it is redirected somewhere else, such as by the IGP or another LSP. The Drop-Upon-Invalid behaviour is the opposite: the LSP keeps attracting traffic and the traffic is dropped at the headend. Such an LSP is said to be in drop state, and while in that state the LSP operational state is UP, as indicated by the O-flag in the LSP object, although the ERO object may be empty if no valid path has been computed. The TLV is used in both directions between PCEP peers: the PCE tells the PCC whether to enable or disable Drop-Upon-Invalid, and the PCC reports the current setting and whether the LSP is currently in the drop state. The TLV has type 70 and a length of 4, with an Oper flag octet in which bit 7 is the Dropping flag, set to zero by the PCE and ignored by the PCC, and a Config flag octet in which bit 7 is the Drop enabled flag.

Drop-Upon-Invalid is enabled on the whole SR Policy rather than on a particular Candidate Path: if any Candidate Path has it enabled, the whole policy has the feature enabled. An SR Policy is invalid when all its Candidate Paths are invalid. Once all the Candidate Paths of an SR Policy have become invalid, the policy checks whether any of them have Drop-Upon-Invalid enabled; if so, the policy enters the drop state and activates the highest preference Candidate Path that has the feature enabled. Only one Candidate Path then needs to be reported to the PCE with the Dropping flag set.
sections.plainLanguage: Three settings travel on the path itself. The first says how urgently the controller should recompute the path when the network changes. The second says whether an unlabelled IP packet gets an Explicit NULL label pushed on it so that it can enter the policy in the MPLS data plane. The third decides what happens when the path breaks: normally the traffic is sent somewhere else, but with this setting the path keeps attracting traffic and the traffic is dropped at the headend instead, which is what an operator wants for a path that must not silently divert.

sections.title: Security and Manageability Considerations
sections.content:
The information carried in the new SRPA object and TLVs could give an eavesdropper additional information about the SR Policy. The security considerations described in RFC 5440, RFC 8231, RFC 8281, RFC 8664, RFC 8697, RFC 9256 and RFC 9603 apply to this specification.

As recommended in RFC 8231, these PCEP extensions should be activated only on authenticated and encrypted sessions between PCEs and PCCs belonging to the same administrative authority, using Transport Layer Security as recommended by the best current practices in RFC 9325.

On manageability, all the requirements of RFC 5440, RFC 8231, RFC 8664, RFC 9256 and RFC 9603 apply. In addition, an implementation must allow the operator to view the SR Policy Identifier and the SR Policy Candidate Path Identifier advertised in an association object, and should allow the operator to view the capabilities defined here that each PCEP peer has advertised, and to view the LSPs associated with a specific SR Policy Identifier. A PCE or PCC implementation may allow the capabilities and the SRPA support to be enabled and disabled.
sections.plainLanguage: The new objects carry details about the policy, so an eavesdropper learns something new. The document therefore recommends that these extensions run only over sessions that are authenticated and encrypted, between devices under the same administration. It also requires that an operator can see the policy identifiers and the paths belonging to a policy, so that a working setup can be checked.
